score.scale: 0-100, higher means more risk. 0-29 low, 30-59 elevated, 60-84 high, 85-100 critical.
score.disclaimer: Automated risk estimate based on detected issues. Not legal advice and not a prediction or guarantee of any legal outcome.

checks.label: Buttons and links have accessible names
Form fields have labels and clear errors
"Do Not Sell or Share" opt-out and Global Privacy Control
Cookie banner offers a real choice
GDPR: privacy notice lists legal bases and rights
European Accessibility Act: accessibility information published

issues.title: Your "Add to cart" button has no name a screen reader can read
issues.plainEnglish: Blind shoppers using a screen reader hear "button" and nothing else, so they can't tell how to buy.
issues.whySued: Being unable to complete a purchase is the kind of barrier website accessibility complaints describe most often.
issues.howToFix: Give the icon button a text label, e.g. aria-label="Add to cart", or put visible text inside it.
issues.standard: WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (Level A)

issues.title: Meta and TikTok pixels fire before the visitor makes a cookie choice
issues.plainEnglish: Your ad trackers send visitor data the moment the page loads, before anyone clicks Accept.
issues.whySued: Sharing visitor data with ad platforms without consent has been the basis of US privacy lawsuits and regulator actions.
issues.howToFix: Load pixels through your consent manager so they only fire after opt-in, and honor Global Privacy Control signals.

issues.title: Checkout form fields have no labels
issues.plainEnglish: Placeholder text disappears when someone starts typing, and screen readers can't tell which box is which.
issues.whySued: A checkout a disabled customer can't fill in blocks them from buying, which is the core of most website accessibility claims.
issues.howToFix: Add a visible <label> tied to every input, and announce errors in text, not color alone.

issues.title: 41 product images have no alt text
issues.plainEnglish: Screen reader users can't tell what your products look like.
issues.whySued: Missing image descriptions are among the barriers most commonly cited in website accessibility complaints.
issues.howToFix: Write short, specific alt text for product photos, and use alt="" for decorative images.

issues.title: No "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" link
issues.plainEnglish: California visitors have no way to opt out of their data being shared for ads.
issues.whySued: Regulators have enforced missing opt-outs and ignored Global Privacy Control under the CCPA.
issues.howToFix: Add the opt-out link in your footer, wire it to your consent tool, and honor GPC browser signals.

issues.title: The menu can't be opened with a keyboard
issues.plainEnglish: People who can't use a mouse can't reach your categories or your cart.
issues.whySued: Keyboard traps and unreachable navigation block entire sites for some disabled users.
issues.howToFix: Use a real <button> for the menu toggle, and make sure Tab reaches every link with a visible focus ring.

issues.title: Privacy policy is missing required disclosures
issues.plainEnglish: Your policy doesn't say which data you collect, who you share it with, or how people can delete it.
issues.whySued: Incomplete privacy notices are a common basis for regulator inquiries and demand letters.
issues.howToFix: Use the Compliantfy policy generator, then have counsel review it.

issues.title: Light gray text is too faint to read
issues.plainEnglish: Prices and sale tags fail contrast minimums for people with low vision.
issues.whySued: Low contrast is frequently listed alongside other barriers in accessibility complaints.
issues.howToFix: Raise text contrast to at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text).

issues.title: No accessibility statement or contact for access problems
issues.plainEnglish: Visitors who hit a barrier have no way to ask you for help.
issues.whySued: Without a contact route, a frustrated user's next step may be a lawyer instead of you.
issues.howToFix: Publish an accessibility statement with a phone number and email for help.
issues.standard: Best practice; EAA requires accessibility information in the EU

issues.title: Content-Security-Policy header is missing
issues.plainEnglish: Your site is easier to tamper with through injected scripts.
issues.whySued: Not a common lawsuit trigger on its own, but it's part of a reasonable security posture.
issues.howToFix: Add a Content-Security-Policy header at your host or CDN.

issues.title: Analytics cookies are set before consent for EU visitors
issues.plainEnglish: EU visitors get tracking cookies before they agree.
issues.whySued: EU regulators require prior consent for non-essential cookies.
issues.howToFix: Block non-essential cookies until opt-in for EU traffic, and add a Reject button with equal weight.

issues.title: No accessibility information for EU customers
issues.plainEnglish: If you sell to EU consumers, the European Accessibility Act expects you to publish how your service meets accessibility requirements.
issues.whySued: EAA obligations apply from June 2025, and enforcement is by EU member-state authorities.
issues.howToFix: Publish an accessibility statement covering EU requirements, and fix WCAG issues.

recommendation.reason: 6 critical issues across checkout and tracking. Fixes touch theme code and the consent setup.

euSummary.note: EU module is scored separately and is not included in score or summary.
